planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; propagate by softwood cuttings in early summer since this species is rarely seed-grown in cultivation.

directions: Native to open woodland and scrub in Yunnan and Sichuan, this Chinese species forms a dense, rounded mound noticeably smaller than D. scabra or D. gracilis. Clusters of small white flowers open along the branches in late spring to early summer, set against narrow, finely toothed leaves. It stays tidy with little pruning beyond removing a few of the oldest stems after flowering, and tolerates average garden soil once established.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; increase by softwood or semi-ripe cuttings taken in summer.

directions: Native to central China, this upright, arching species carries star-shaped white flowers in early summer, with petals sometimes faintly flushed pink on the reverse. Like many Chinese shrub discoveries bearing this epithet, it commemorates the plant hunter Ernest Henry Wilson, who introduced numerous deutzias to Western gardens in the early twentieth century. The leaves and young stems carry the characteristic stellate hairs of the genus, giving a slightly rough texture to the touch. It is less widely offered than D. gracilis or D. scabra but worth seeking out where a taller, later-blooming species deutzia is wanted.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; root softwood cuttings in early summer, and prune right after flowering since bloom forms on the previous year's wood.

directions: Native to Honshu, Japan, this species produces unusually dark, funnel-shaped flowers in deep red to maroon-crimson, among the richest flower color found in wild weigela species rather than the more common pinks of W. florida. Blooms open along arching stems in late spring, drawing hummingbirds and other nectar feeders. Because of its saturated flower color, it has been used by breeders as a parent in developing dark-red garden weigela selections. Give it the same full-sun, well-drained siting and post-bloom pruning as other weigelas to keep its naturally loose, spreading habit in check.
sources: Bean's Trees and Shrubs Hardy in the British Isles

planting.note: Plant in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; propagate by cuttings, and prune immediately after flowering to shape next year's growth.

directions: Found wild from Hokkaido south through Honshu, Japan, this species bears rose-pink to deep pink funnel flowers held in pairs along the branches in mid-to-late spring, slightly ahead of many W. florida selections. It was long grown in Japanese gardens before Western breeders drew on it to broaden the color range of ornamental weigela hybrids. The arching branches and dense twiggy growth make it useful as an informal flowering hedge or border shrub. Water regularly the first season to establish a deep root system, after which it tolerates average garden conditions.

planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this Korean species tolerates colder winters than many garden weigela selections.

directions: Native to Korea, this compact species opens flowers in a pale yellow-green that gradually shifts through pink to rosy red as each bloom ages, so a single cluster can show three colors at once. It has been included in cold-hardiness trials at botanical collections because of its ability to handle harsher winters than W. florida. Its smaller, denser habit suits foundation plantings or mixed borders where a looser weigela would outgrow the space. Little pruning is needed beyond removing old wood after flowering to encourage fresh growth.

planting.note: Plant in a rock garden or raised bed with sharp drainage in full sun; its small size makes it unsuitable for the heavy pruning regimes used on larger forsythias.

directions: Restricted in the wild to the Izu Peninsula and nearby Izu Islands of Japan, this is one of the smallest members of the forsythia genus, forming a low, twiggy mound rather than the tall arching fountain of the common garden hybrids. Its early-spring flowers are noticeably paler than the familiar bright gold of F. x intermedia, running toward cream to very pale yellow, and open on bare stems ahead of the foliage. Because of its diminutive size it has mostly been grown by rock-garden and alpine plant enthusiasts rather than in mainstream shrub borders. Give it the gritty, sharply drained soil typical of rock-garden plantings rather than the rich, moist ground that suits larger forsythias.
